item.title: Hagi Castle Town: Samurai Streets and Meiji History — Guide
item.description: Hagi is one of Japan’s best-preserved castle towns, a quiet grid of streets on the Sea of Japan coast where whole quarters of samurai and merchant houses survive behind long earthen walls, summer oranges hanging over the lanes. Once the castle seat of the powerful Mori clan, Hagi became a cradle of the Meiji Restoration, the movement that overthrew the shogunate and founded modern Japan — its private academy schooled several of the new nation’s founding leaders, and the town’s industrial heritage sites are UNESCO-listed.

item.title: Kazurabashi: The Iya Valley Vine Bridge — Guide
item.description: The Kazurabashi is one of the last surviving vine bridges in Japan, a remarkable suspension bridge in the Iya Valley woven entirely from the tough stems of mountain kiwi vines. Bridges like this once crossed the valley’s many gorges, built from natural materials that could be cut down quickly — legend says to foil pursuers in this refuge of defeated warriors. Around 45 metres long and swaying gently above the clear Iya River, the bridge is rebuilt every few years to keep it safe, but crossing it is still a genuine thrill: the vine ropes creak, the wooden slats are spaced with gaps you can see the water through, and the whole span moves as you go.

item.title: Kintaikyo Bridge: Iwakuni's Five Wooden Arches — Guide
item.description: The Kintaikyo is one of Japan’s three most famous bridges and among its most beautiful, a series of five elegant wooden arches sweeping across the wide Nishiki River at Iwakuni in eastern Yamaguchi. First built in the seventeenth century and faithfully rebuilt to the same design, its arches are constructed with intricate interlocking joinery and famously use almost no nails. You can walk across the bridge itself, its wooden treads rising and falling beneath your feet, while the riverbanks are lined with cherry trees that turn the scene pink in spring.

item.title: Myozen-ji Temple — Guide
item.description: Myozen-ji is a historic Buddhist temple in Kumamoto, offering a calm and atmospheric stop away from the main tourist trail. Its aged wooden main hall, temple gate, statues and gardens carry the quiet dignity of a long-established place of worship, and the grounds change with the seasons — blossom in spring, cool green in summer, and coloured foliage in autumn. Like many of Kumamoto’s neighbourhood temples, it invites visitors to slow down, wander the peaceful precincts, admire the traditional architecture and enjoy a moment of stillness.
